listen_text: Section. Introduction. In the source passage on chap and the source passage on chap , we developed a theory of cardinals by treating cardinals as ordinals. That approach depends upon the Axiom of Well-Ordering. It turns out that Well-Ordering is equivalent to another principle—the Axiom of Choice—and there has been serious philosophical discussion of its acceptability. Our question for this chapter are: How is the Axiom used, and can it be justified? End section.

Section. The Tarski—Scott Trick. In the source passage on defcardinalasordinal , we defined cardinals as ordinals. To do this, we assumed the Axiom of Well-Ordering. We did this, for no other reason than that it is the “industry standard”. Before we discuss any of the philosophical issues surrounding Well-Ordering, then, it is important to be clear that we can depart from the industry standard, and develop a theory of cardinals without assuming Well-Ordering. We can still employ the definitions of capital A is equinumerous with capital B , capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B and capital A has smaller cardinality than capital B , as they appeared in the source passage on chap . We will just need a new notion of cardinal. A naïve thought would be to attempt to define capital A apostrophe s cardinality thus: Displayed expression. the set of x such that capital A is equinumerous with x. End displayed expression. You might want to compare this with Frege's definition of the number determined by x applied to Fx , sketched at the very end of the source passage on sec . And, for reasons we gestured at there, this definition fails. Any singleton set is equinumerous with the set containing the empty set . But new singleton sets are formed at every successor stage of the hierarchy (just consider the singleton of the previous stage). So the set of x such that capital A is equinumerous with x does not exist, since it cannot have a rank. To get around this problem, we use a trick due to Tarski and Scott: Footnote. A reminder: all formulas may have parameters (unless explicitly stated otherwise). End footnote. Definition. Tarski—Scott. End definition. We should check that this definition is legitimate. Working in set theory Z F , the source passage on zfentailsregularity guarantees that the rank of x exists for every x . Having justified the Tarski—Scott trick, we can now use it to define a notion of cardinality: Definition. The ts -cardinality of capital A is the T S cardinality of capital A equals the Tarski Scott set of all x of least possible rank that are equinumerous with capital A . End definition. The definition of a ts -cardinal does not use Well-Ordering. But, even without that Axiom, we can show that ts -cardinals behave rather like cardinals as defined in the source passage on defcardinalasordinal . For example, if we restate the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right and the lemma on Size Powersettwo Exp in terms of ts -cardinals, the proofs go through just fine in set theory Z F , without assuming Well-Ordering. listen_text: Section. The Well-Ordering Problem. Evidently rather a lot hangs on whether we accept Well-Ordering. But the discussion of this principle has tended to focus on an equivalent principle, the Axiom of Choice. So we will now turn our attention to that (and prove the equivalence). In the cited work by Cantor from one eight eight three , Cantor expressed his support for the Axiom of Well-Ordering, calling it “a law of thought which appears to me to be fundamental, rich in its consequences, and particularly remarkable for its general validity” (cited in the cited work by Potter from twenty hundred four the cited work by Potter from twenty hundred four ). But Cantor ultimately became convinced that the “Axiom” was in need of proof. So did the mathematical community. The problem was “solved” by Zermelo in the cited work by Zermelo from nineteen hundred four . To explain his solution, we need some definitions. Definition. A function f is a choice function if and only if f of x belongs to x for all x belongs to the domain of f . We say that f is a choice function for capital A if and only if f is a choice function with the domain of f equals capital A set minus the set containing the empty set . End definition. Intuitively, for every (non-empty) set x belongs to capital A , a choice function for capital A chooses a particular element, f of x , from x . The Axiom of Choice is then: Axiom. Choice. Every set has a choice function. End axiom. Zermelo showed that Choice entails well-ordering, and vice versa: Theorem. in set theory Z F . Well-Ordering and Choice are equivalent. End theorem. Proof. Left-to-right. Let capital A be a set of sets. Then the union of capital A exists by the Axiom of Union, and so by Well-Ordering there is some is less than which well-orders the union of capital A . Now let f of x equals the less than least member of x with respect to the preceding less than ordering . This is a choice function for capital A . Right-to-left. Fix capital A . That is, when capital A equals the image of alpha under g for the first time, let g of delta equals capital A for all delta is less than or equal to alpha . Now, in the first instance, we can only be sure that this defines a term (see the remarks after the source passage on transrecursionschema ); but we will show that we indeed have a function. Since f is a choice function, for each alpha (when defined) we have g of alpha equals f of capital A set minus the image of alpha under g belongs to capital A set minus the image of alpha under g ; that is, g of alpha does not belong to the image of alpha under g . So if g of alpha equals g of beta then g of beta does not belong to the image of alpha under g , that is, beta does not belong to alpha , and similarly alpha does not belong to beta . So alpha equals beta , by Trichotomy. So g is injective. Next, observe that we do stop!, that is that there is some (least) ordinal alpha such that capital A equals the image of alpha under g . For suppose otherwise; then as g is injective we would have alpha has smaller cardinality than the power set of capital A set minus the set containing the empty set for every ordinal alpha , contradicting the source passage on Hartogs Lemma . So Well-Ordering and Choice stand or fall together. But the question remains: do they stand or fall? End section.

This is a special case of Choice. And it transpires that this principle was invoked fairly frequently, without an obvious awareness of its use. Here are two nice examples. Footnote. It is used to choose our sequence of functions f subscript zero , f subscript one , f subscript two , and so on Footnote. A similar use of Choice occurred in the source passage on kappaunionkappasize , when we gave the instruction “For each beta belongs to the cardinal a , fix an injection f subscript beta ”. End footnote. And again, the result fails in the absence of any Choice principle. Specifically, the cited work by Feferman, Levy from nineteen hundred sixty three proved that it is consistent with set theory Z F that a countable union of countable sets has cardinality beth subscript one . But here is a much funnier statement of the point, from Russell: Quotation. This is illustrated by the millionaire who bought a pair of socks whenever he bought a pair of boots, and never at any other time, and who had such a passion for buying both that at last he had aleph subscript zero pairs of boots and aleph subscript zero pairs of socks and so on Among boots we can distinguish right and left, and therefore we can make a selection of one out of each pair, namely, we can choose all the right boots or all the left boots; but with socks no such principle of selection suggests itself, and we cannot be sure, unless we assume the multiplicative axiom Open bracket. That is, in effect Choice. Close bracket., that there is any class consisting of one sock out of each pair. the cited work by Russell from nineteen hundred nineteen End quotation. In short, some form of Choice is needed to prove the following: If you have countably many pairs of socks, then you have (only) countably many socks. And in fact, without Countable Choice (or something equivalent), a countable union of countable sets can fail to be countable. End example. The moral is that Countable Choice was used repeatedly, without much awareness of its users. The philosophical question is: How could we justify Countable Choice? An attempt at an intuitive justification might invoke an appeal to a supertask. Suppose we make the first choice in the fraction one over two a minute, our second choice in the fraction one over four a minute, and so on, our n indexed choice in the fraction one over two superscript n a minute, and so on Then within one minute, we will have made an omega -sequence of choices, and defined a choice function. But what, really, could such a thought-experiment tell us? For a start, it relies upon taking this idea of “choosing” rather literally. For another, it seems to bind up mathematics in metaphysical possibility. More important: it is not going to give us any justification for Choice tout court, rather than mere Countable Choice. For if we need every set to have a choice function, then we'll need to be able to perform a “supertask of arbitrary ordinal length.” Bluntly, that idea is laughable. End section.

listen_text: Section. Intrinsic Considerations about Choice. The broader question, then, is whether Well-Ordering, or Choice, or indeed the comparability of all sets as regards their size—it doesn't matter which—can be justified. Here is an attempted intrinsic justification. Back in the source passage on sec , we introduced several principles about the hierarchy. One of these is worth restating: List. Next item.. Stages accumulate. For any stage capital S , and for any sets which were formed before stage capital S : a set is formed at stage capital S whose members are exactly those sets. Nothing else is formed at stage capital S . End list. In fact, many authors have suggested that the Axiom of Choice can be justified via (something like) this principle. We will briefly provide a gloss on that approach. We will start with a simple little result, which offers yet another equivalent for Choice: Theorem. in set theory Z F . Choice is equivalent to the following principle. If the elements of capital A are disjoint and non-empty, then there is some capital C such that capital C intersected with x is a singleton for every x belongs to capital A . (We call such a capital C a choice set for capital A .) End theorem. The proof of this result is straightforward, and we leave it as an exercise for the reader. Exercise. Prove the source passage on choiceset . If you struggle, you can find a proof in the cited work by Potter from twenty hundred four . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. The essential point is that a choice set for capital A is just the range of a choice function for capital A . So, to justify Choice, we can simply try to justify its equivalent formulation, in terms of the existence of choice sets. And we will now try to do exactly that. Let capital A apostrophe s elements be disjoint and non-empty. By Stages are key (see the source passage on sec ), capital A is formed at some stage capital S . Note that all the elements of the union of capital A are available before stage capital S . Now, by Stages accumulate, for any sets which were formed before capital S , a set is formed whose members are exactly those sets. Otherwise put: every possible collections of earlier-available sets will exist at capital S . But it is certainly possible to select objects which could be formed into a choice set for capital A ; that is just some very specific subset of the union of capital A . So: some such choice set exists, as required. Well, that's a very quick attempt to offer a justification of Choice on intrinsic grounds. But, to pursue this idea further, you should read Potter's ( the cited work by Potter from twenty hundred four ) neat development of it. End section.

listen_text: Section. The Banach—Tarski Paradox. We might also attempt to justify Choice, as Boolos attempted to justify Replacement, by appealing to extrinsic considerations (see the source passage on sec ). After all, adopting Choice has many desirable consequences: the ability to compare every cardinal; the ability to well-order every set; the ability to treat cardinals as a particular kind of ordinal; etc. Sometimes, however, it is claimed that Choice has undesirable consequences. Mostly, this is due to a result by the cited work by Banach, Tarski from nineteen hundred twenty four . Theorem. Banach—Tarski Paradox (in set theory Z F C ). Any ball can be decomposed into finitely many pieces, which can be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form two copies of that ball. End theorem. At first glance, this is a bit amazing. Clearly the two balls have twice the volume of the original ball. But rigid motions—rotation and transportation—do not change volume. So it looks as if Banach—Tarski allows us to magick new matter into existence. It gets worse. Footnote. See the cited work by Wagon from twenty hundred sixteen . End footnote. Similar reasoning shows that a pea can be cut into finitely many pieces, which can then be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form an entity the shape and size of Big Ben. None of this, however, holds in set theory Z F on its own. Footnote. Though Banach—Tarski can be proved with principles which are strictly weaker than Choice; see the cited work by Wagon from twenty hundred sixteen . End footnote. So we face a decision: reject Choice, or learn to live with the “paradox”. We're going to suggest that we should learn to live with the “paradox”. listen_text: Section. Appendix: Vitali's Paradox. To get a real sense of whether the Banach-Tarski construction is acceptable or not, we should examine its proof. Unfortunately, that would require much more algebra than we can present here. However, we can offer some quick remarks which might shed some insight on the proof of Banach-Tarski, Footnote. For a much fuller treatment, see the cited work by Weston from twenty hundred three or the cited work by Wagon from twenty hundred sixteen . End footnote. by focussing on the following result: Theorem. Vitali's Paradox (in set theory Z F C ). Any circle can be decomposed into countably many pieces, which can be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form two copies of that circle. End theorem. Vitali's Paradox is much easier to prove than the Banach—Tarski Paradox. We have called it “Vitali's Paradox”, since it follows from Vitali's the cited work by Vitali from nineteen hundred five construction of an unmeasurable set. But the set-theoretic aspects of the proof of Vitali's Paradox and the Banach-Tarski Paradox are very similar. The essential difference between the results is just that Banach-Tarski considers a finite decomposition, whereas Vitali's Paradox considers a countably infinite decomposition. As the cited work by Weston from twenty hundred three puts it, Vitali's Paradox “is certainly not nearly as striking as the Banach—Tarski paradox, but it does illustrate that geometric paradoxes can happen even in `simple' situations.” Vitali's Paradox concerns a two-dimensional figure, a circle. So we will work on the plane, the real numbers superscript two . Let the group of rotations of the unit circle be the set of (clockwise) rotations of points around the origin by rational radian values between the half open interval from zero inclusive to two pi exclusive . Here are some algebraic facts about the group of rotations of the unit circle (if you don't understand the statement of the result, the proof will make its meaning clear): Lemma. the group of rotations of the unit circle forms an abelian group under composition of functions. End lemma. Proof. For we can generate two copies of the unit circle from the unit circle , just by splitting it up into countably many pieces (the various the image of capital C under rho apostrophe s ) and then rigidly moving them (simply rotate each piece of capital D subscript one , and first transport and then rotate each piece of capital D subscript two ). Let's recap the proof-strategy. We started with some algebraic facts about the group of rotations on the plane. We used this group to partition the unit circle into equivalence classes. We then arrived at a “paradox”, by using Choice to select elements from each class. We use exactly the same strategy to prove Banach—Tarski. The main difference is that the algebraic facts used to prove Banach—Tarski are significantly more complicated than those used to prove Vitali's Paradox. But those algebraic facts have nothing to do with Choice. We will summarise them quickly. To prove Banach—Tarski, we start by establishing an analogue of the source passage on disjointgroup : any free group can be split into four pieces, which intuitively we can “move around” to recover two copies of the whole group. Footnote. The fact that we can use four pieces is due to the cited work by Robinson from nineteen hundred forty seven . For a recent proof, see the cited work by Wagon from twenty hundred sixteen . We follow the cited work by Weston from twenty hundred three in describing this as “moving” the pieces of the group. End footnote. We then show that we can use two particular rotations around the origin of the real numbers superscript three to generate a free group of rotations, capital F . Footnote. See the cited work by Wagon from twenty hundred sixteen . End footnote. (No Choice yet.) We now regard points on the surface of the sphere as “similar” if and only if one can be obtained from the other by a rotation in capital F . We then use Choice to select exactly one point from each equivalence class of “similar” points. Applying our division of capital F to the surface of the sphere, as in the source passage on pseudobanachtarski , we split that surface into four pieces, which we can “move around” to obtain two copies of the surface of the sphere. And this establishes the cited work by Hausdorff from nineteen hundred fourteen : Theorem. Hausdorff's Paradox (in set theory Z F C ). The surface of any sphere can be decomposed into finitely many pieces, which can be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form two disjoint copies of that sphere. End theorem. A couple of further algebraic tricks are needed to obtain the full Banach-Tarski Theorem (which concerns not just the sphere's surface, but its interior too). Frankly, however, this is just icing on the algebraic cake. Hence Weston writes: Quotation. Open bracket. Ellipsis. From this point of view, the Banach-Tarski paradox is not a statement about the real numbers superscript three so much as it is a statement about the complexity of the group Open bracket. Of translations and rotations in the real numbers superscript three . Close bracket.. the cited work by Weston from twenty hundred three End quotation. That is: whether we can offer a finite decomposition (as in Banach—Tarski) or a countably infinite decomposition (as in Vitali's Paradox) comes down to certain group-theoretic facts about working in two-dimension or three-dimensions. Admittedly, this last observation slightly spoils the joke at the end of the source passage on sec . Since it is two dimensional, “Banach-Tarski” must be divided into a countable infinity of pieces, if one wants to rearrange those pieces to form “Banach-Tarski Banach-Tarski”. To repair the joke, one must write in three dimensions. We leave this as an exercise for the reader. One final comment.
